inequality-s3.text: Placeholder scenario: a lighthouse signal guides every passing ship, and one ship seeing it does not stop another from seeing it.

items.q: Placeholder: what does a Lorenz curve show?
options: The price of a good at each quantity
The output a firm makes with each worker
The cost of each extra unit
The share of income held by each share of households

why.correct: Placeholder: cumulative households against cumulative income.
options: Right: cumulative income by cumulative households.

items.q: Placeholder: a per-unit tax is placed on sellers. Shade the tax revenue.

why.correct: Placeholder: the rectangle between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep, out to the quantity after the tax.

slips.dwl: Placeholder: that triangle is the deadweight loss; the revenue is the rectangle.

items.q: Placeholder: label the axes and both curves of the inequality graph.

why.correct: Placeholder: cumulative households across, cumulative income up, the diagonal and the bowed curve.

items.q: Placeholder: a tax cuts the quantity traded from 50 to 40 and opens a price wedge of 4 dollars. What is the deadweight loss, in dollars?

why.correct: Placeholder: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 4 = 20$.

mistakes.why: Placeholder: that is the rectangle; the deadweight loss is a triangle, so take one half.

items.q: Placeholder: a tax takes a larger share of income from people with higher incomes. Which kind of tax is it?

why.correct: Placeholder: the share rises with income.
options: The share would stay the same.
The share would fall with income.
Right: the share rises with income.
A lump-sum tax is the same amount for all.

items.q: Placeholder: according to the table, what share of income does the poorest fifth hold?

why.correct: Placeholder: read the first row, where the poorest fifth holds $20\%$ of the income it would hold with equal shares.
options: That is the second fifth's share.
That is the cumulative share of the poorest two fifths plus more.

items.q: Placeholder: what cumulative percent of income do the poorest two fifths hold?

why.correct: Placeholder: $5 + 15 = 20$.

mistakes.why: Placeholder: 15 is the second fifth alone; add the first fifth.

items.q: Placeholder: which fifths hold more than an equal share of income? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Placeholder: an equal share is 20%.

items.q: Placeholder: if every fifth held 20%, where would the Lorenz curve lie?

why.correct: Placeholder: equal shares make the curve the diagonal.
options: Right: it would be the diagonal.
That would mean no one has income.
A Lorenz curve never rises above it.

items.q: Placeholder: in the graph, which area is the deadweight loss of the subsidy?

why.correct: Placeholder: between supply and demand, beyond the efficient quantity.
options: Area a is consumer surplus before the subsidy.

items.q: Placeholder: in the graph, which areas together are the cost of the subsidy?
options: b, c, e, f and g

why.correct: Placeholder: the whole rectangle out to the new quantity.
options: That leaves out c, f and g.

items.q: Placeholder: in the graph, what happens to the quantity traded after the subsidy?

why.correct: Placeholder: supply shifts right.
options: Right: the new crossing is further right.

items.q: Placeholder: build the answer: why does a monopolist charge more than marginal cost?

why.correct: Placeholder: it produces where MR = MC and reads the price from demand, which lies above MR.

specific.frame: It produces where ___ equals ___, and reads its price from ___.
specific.model: Placeholder: it produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, because the next unit would add more to cost than to revenue, and reads its price from the demand curve above that quantity, which is higher than marginal cost.

why.1: Placeholder: price equals MC is the efficient rule, not the monopolist's.
Placeholder: the price comes from demand, not from MR.

items.q: Placeholder: put the long-run steps in order after a rise in demand in a competitive market.
options: Price falls back to minimum ATC

why.correct: Placeholder: each step causes the next.

items.q: Placeholder: in the scenario, which kind of good is the lighthouse signal?
options: A club good sold by subscription

why.correct: Placeholder: nonrival and nonexcludable.
options: It is not rival or excludable.

items.q: Placeholder: in the scenario, why will few ships pay for the signal?
options: They can use it without paying
The signal is too costly to see
The price is set by MR

why.correct: Placeholder: the free-rider problem.

items.q: Placeholder: in the scenario, who is likely to provide the signal?
options: The ship with the most cargo

why.correct: Placeholder: public goods are often provided by government.
options: One ship would bear the whole cost.
Cargo does not change free riding.

items.q: Placeholder: mark the monopolist's price and quantity.

why.correct: Placeholder: the quantity where MR = MC, the price up on demand.

items.q: Placeholder: demand rises in a competitive market. Shift the right curve and draw the firm's new price line.

why.correct: Placeholder: market demand shifts right; the firm takes the higher price.

items.q: Placeholder: mark each firm's dominant strategy, if any, and every Nash equilibrium.

why.correct: Placeholder: Firm A's dominant strategy is Low; Firm B has none; the Nash equilibrium is (Low, Low).

items.q: Placeholder: shade the monopsonist's wage bill.

why.correct: Placeholder: the wage read from labor supply times the workers hired.

items.q: Placeholder: mark the socially efficient quantity and price.

why.correct: Placeholder: where marginal social benefit meets marginal social cost.

items.q: Placeholder: which change makes the Lorenz curve bow further from the line of equality?
options: A transfer to the poorest households
A larger share of income for the richest fifth

why.correct: Placeholder: more income at the top means more inequality.
options: Right: the curve bows further out.
That is the line of equality itself.
